scope.topic: Periodic Properties & their variations in Groups & Periods
points: Definitions & trends of the following periodic properties in groups & periods should be studied:

scope.topic: Periodicity on the basis of atomic number for elements
points: Study of modern periodic table up to period 4 (no questions on elements beyond period 4 - Calcium)
Periodicity & other related properties explained on basis of nuclear charge & shells (not orbitals)
Special reference to the alkali metals & halogen groups
Groups numbered 1 to 18 (IUPAC notation) and IA-VIIA, VIII, IB-VIIB & 0 (older notation accepted)

syllabus_scope.IUPAC_note: According to IUPAC recommendation, the GROUPS are numbered from 1 to 18 - replacing older notation. Both notations accepted for examination.

key_formulas_and_equations.equation: Properties of elements = Periodic functions of their Atomic Numbers (Z)
M⁺(g) + Energy (2nd I.P.) → M²⁺(g) + e⁻  [2nd I.P. > 1st I.P.]
X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g) + Energy (E.A.)  [e.g. Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻, −3.80 eV]
M → M⁺ + e⁻  (Metal acts as Electron Donor / Reducing Agent)
N + e⁻ → N⁻  (Non-metal acts as Electron Acceptor / Oxidising Agent)
n/p ≈ 1.0 (Stable Light Metals)  |  n/p > 1.5 (Radioactive Heavy Elements)

section_A_introduction.title: Introduction & History of Classification
need_for_classification: Need arose to group elements into families whose elements showed maximum resemblance.
On such an arrangement in the form of a table, properties of elements were seen to reappear at regular intervals.

history_of_classification.outcome: Method discarded as elements showed variable valency and dual character.
Elements arranged in groups of three called TRIADS. Atomic weight of the middle element was generally the average of the other two. Discarded as it did not hold true for all elements.
Elements arranged in a series of eight. Properties of every eighth element were a repetition of the first (Law of Octaves). Discarded as it failed to leave spaces for undiscovered elements.

Elements arranged in the form of a table called Mendeleeff's Periodic Table. Stated that properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic weights. Could not justify position of certain elements, rare earths and isotopes.

Elements arranged in a modified table called Modern Periodic Table. Stated that properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Removes most defects of Mendeleeff's Periodic Table.

section_B_modern_periodic_table.title: Modern Periodic Table - Long form of the Periodic Table
introduction: Mendeleeff had arranged elements in the periodic table on basis of increasing atomic weights.

Moseley modified Mendeleeff's periodic table & stated that the basis of classification of elements should be increasing atomic numbers (not atomic weights) since physical and chemical properties of elements depend on the number of electrons and their arrangement.
Atomic number is equal to the number of electrons in the energy shells of an atom - hence atomic number is the fundamental property of an element.
section_B_modern_periodic_table.modern_periodic_law: Physical & chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

salient_features.description: Periodic table based on basic fundamental property - atomic number.
Correlates position of an element with its electronic configuration.
Arranges elements in increasing order of atomic numbers in SEVEN horizontal rows called PERIODS & EIGHTEEN vertical columns called GROUPS.

Completion of each period is logical - each period begins with an element having one electron in outermost shell & ends with zero group element having completely filled outer shell. A transition from metallic to non-metallic character is seen across a period.

Each vertical column accommodates elements with the same outer electronic configuration, hence having similar properties. 18 vertical columns consist of groups 1 to 17 & 18 [zero group]. Groups 1, 2 & 13 to 17 [IA to VIIA] are called NORMAL ELEMENTS. Groups 3 to 12 [IB to VIIB & VIII] are called TRANSITION ELEMENTS. Group 18 [zero] at extreme right contains NOBLE or INERT GASES.
Reactive metals placed in group 1 [IA] and 2 [IIA]. Transition elements [metals] placed in the middle. Non-metals placed in the upper right corner of the periodic table.

Gradual change in properties is seen with increase in atomic number. Periodicity in properties (recurrence of properties) is seen with elements of the same subgroup after a difference of 2, 8, 18 or 32 in atomic numbers - due to recurrence of similar valence shell electronic configuration.

section_C_periods.title: Periods in the Modern Periodic Table
key_concepts: Periods = Seven horizontal rows of elements arranged in increasing order of atomic numbers.
Period numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) signify the NUMBER OF ELECTRON SHELLS of an element.
Period 1 elements (e.g. 1H) have 1 shell; Period 2 elements (e.g. 3Li) have 2 shells; Period 3 elements (e.g. 11Na) have 3 shells, and so on.
section_C_periods.dual_position_of_hydrogen: Hydrogen has the simplest electronic configuration of one. It can hence lose 1 electron, behaving like alkali metals (group 1) OR gain 1 electron, behaving like halogens (group 17). It is hence placed above Li in group 1 OR above F in group 17.
section_C_periods.isotopes_of_hydrogen: Atoms of the same element, having same atomic number but different atomic mass numbers. Hydrogen exists in 3 isotopic forms: 1H, 2H, 3H. Since they have the same electronic configuration, they occupy the same position in the periodic table.

bridge_elements.definition: Period 2 elements are called 'bridge elements' - they show similarities in properties diagonally with the period 3 element of the next group.
bridge_elements.diagram_ascii:
Period 2:  Li  Be  B  C   (bridge elements)
            ↘   ↘   ↘
Period 3:  Na  Mg  Al  Si  (typical elements)
bridge_elements.example: Li (period 2, group 1) shows diagonal similarity with Mg (period 3, group 2).

property_trends_across_a_period.trend: REMAINS SAME (electrons enter same shell - K, L, M)
INCREASES BY ONE (from left to right)
INCREASES (transition from metallic to non-metallic character)

period_1_elements.note: Noble gas having duplet arrangement of electrons

notes: H2SiO3 = metasilicic acid; HClO4 = perchloric acid; Cl2O7 = chlorine heptoxide
HPO3 = metaphosphoric acid; H3PO4 = orthophosphoric acid

section_D_groups.title: Groups in the Modern Periodic Table
key_concepts: Groups = Eighteen vertical columns (with eight main groups) in the periodic table.
Group numbers signify the NUMBER OF VALENCE ELECTRONS of an element (valence electrons = electrons in outermost shell).
Group 1 (IA) elements e.g. 11Na [2,8,1] have 1 valence electron.
Group 2 (IIA) elements e.g. 12Mg [2,8,2] have 2 valence electrons, and so on.
Transition elements also have 2 valence electrons - e.g. 26Fe [2,8,14,2], 30Zn [2,8,18,2].

groups_summary_table.elements: Heavy metals from 21Sc to 30Zn; 39Y to 48Cd; 72Hf to 80Hg

section_D_groups.inner_transition_elements_note: INNER TRANSITION ELEMENTS (e.g. 58Ce, 90Th) - Metals. Lanthanides (rare earths) & Actinides (radioactive) - two series of 14 elements each. Form two horizontal rows at the bottom of the periodic table. They lie between strongly electropositive metals on the left & least electropositive elements on the right. All have 3 valence electrons (e.g. 21Sc [2,8,8,3]).

property_trends_down_a_subgroup.trend: REMAIN SIMILAR (or vary gradually) - because chemical properties depend on outer electronic configuration

group_1_alkali_metals.elements: Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), Rubidium (Rb), Caesium (Cs), Francium (Fr)
group_1_alkali_metals.nature: Highly reactive, highly electropositive, light, soft metals. Metallic in nature. Soft - can be cut with a knife.
group_1_alkali_metals.redox_nature: Strong reducing agents (alkali metals are electron donors). Have one valence electron easily removed from outer shell. After loss, achieve stable configuration of noble gases.
group_1_alkali_metals.electronegativity: Low electronegativity (electropositive character increases from Li to Cs)

group_17_halogen.nature: Highly reactive, highly electronegative, non-metals. Non-metallic in nature. Gaseous: F & Cl; Liquid: Br; Solid at room temp: I
group_17_halogen.conductivity: Bad or non-conductors of heat & electricity
group_17_halogen.redox_nature: Strong oxidising agents (halogens are electron acceptors). Electronegative character decreases from F to I.
group_17_halogen.reaction_with_non_metals: Covalent compounds formed (e.g. HCl, PCl3, SCl4)
group_17_halogen.reaction_with_hydrogen: Covalent hydrides formed (e.g. HF, HCl, HBr, HI)

section_E_periodic_properties_overview.title: Periodic Properties - Variation in Periods & Groups

periodicity_in_properties.definition: Occurrence of characteristic properties of elements at definite intervals in the modern periodic table when elements are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers. (Definite intervals = difference of 2, 8, 18 or 32 in atomic numbers.)
periodicity_in_properties.modern_periodic_law: Properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

reasons_for_periodicity: After definite intervals of atomic number, similar valence shell electronic configuration occurs.
Properties of elements depend on the number & arrangement of electrons in various shells including valence shell.
In the same period or subgroup, increase or decrease in a particular property is due to gradual change in electronic configuration in the arranged elements.

definitions_table.definition: It is the distance between the centre of the nucleus and the outermost shell of the atom.
It is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
It is the amount of energy released when an atom in the gaseous state accepts an electron to form an anion.
definitions_table.equation: X + e- → X- + energy liberated  [Energy released = E.A.]

definitions_table.definition: It is the tendency of an atom to attract electrons to itself when combined in a compound.
definitions_table.note: Small difference in E.N. between combining atoms → covalent bond. Large difference → ionic bond.

definitions_table.definition: In terms of electron loss or gain: an element is a Non-metal if it gains one or more electrons; a Metal if it loses one or more electrons.

section_F_atomic_size.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Atomic Size
section_F_atomic_size.definition: The distance between the centre of the nucleus of an atom and its outermost shell. (Atomic radius determines bond length.) Unit = Angstrom (Å).

factors_affecting_atomic_size.effect: Increases → Atomic size INCREASES. Reason: distance of outermost shell from nucleus increases.
Increases → Atomic size DECREASES. Reason: electrons in outermost shell are attracted with increasing force. (Nuclear charge = positive charge on nucleus = atomic number of element.)

reasons: Number of shells REMAINS SAME → atomic size unaffected
Nuclear charge INCREASES → atomic size DECREASES

example_period_2.note: Larger than F since outer shell completely filled → force of repulsion; nuclear pull not seen

key_facts: In period 2, Li has the LARGEST atomic radius & F has the SMALLEST.
Neon has a larger atomic radius since in inert gases the outer shell is completely filled, resulting in a force of repulsion. The effect of nuclear pull over valence shell electrons is not seen.
A cation (e.g. Na → Na+ + e-) is SMALLER than the parent neutral atom since the remaining electrons are strongly attracted by the nucleus.

reasons: Number of shells INCREASES → atomic size INCREASES (new shells added with increasing atomic number; nuclear distance from valence electrons increases).
Nuclear charge should increase → atomic size should decrease. BUT
Increase in number of shells DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall atomic radius INCREASES.
trend_down_a_group.important_note: From Li, Na & K - Li has the smallest atomic radius & therefore has higher E.N. & I.P. compared to Na & K. Hence Li has a greater tendency to lose electrons, making it the BEST reducing agent.

section_G_ionisation_potential.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Ionisation Potential (I.P.)
section_G_ionisation_potential.definition: The amount of energy required to remove a loosely bound electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
first_and_second_IP: Energy required to remove 1st electron = FIRST I.P. (M → M+ + e-)  [first I.P. is less]
Energy required to remove 2nd electron = SECOND I.P. (M+ → M2+ + e-)  [second I.P. is more]

factors_affecting_IP.effect: Increases → I.P. DECREASES. Reason: nuclear attraction on outer electrons decreases; outer electrons loosely held.
Increases → I.P. INCREASES. Reason: nuclear attraction on outer electrons increases; outer electrons firmly held.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → I.P. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → I.P. INCREASES
key_facts: Helium (He) has the HIGHEST ionisation potential; Caesium (Cs) has the LOWEST (Francium is radioactive).
Neon in period 2 also has maximum I.P. since its outer shell is completely filled.
Metals lose electrons & generally have LOW ionisation potential compared to non-metals.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → I.P. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → I.P. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall I.P. DECREASES.

section_H_electron_affinity.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Electron Affinity (E.A.)
section_H_electron_affinity.definition: The amount of energy released when an atom in the gaseous state accepts an electron to form an anion.
equations: X + e- → X- + energy liberated  [1st electron affinity]
Cl + e- → Cl-  [−3.80 eV, represented with −ve sign]

factors_affecting_EA.effect: Increases → E.A. DECREASES. Reason: A small atom takes up electrons more readily than a large atom since nucleus has greater attraction on the electrons.
Increases → E.A. INCREASES. Reason: increases the tendency of the atom to accept electrons.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → E.A. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.A. INCREASES
key_facts: Electron affinity is HIGHEST for halogens (group 17) & LEAST for alkali metals (group 1).
Neon (Ne) has electron affinity ZERO since inert gases with stable electronic configuration find it difficult to accept electrons.

INERT GASES DO NOT FORM IONS - their outermost shell is completely filled. They need not accept or donate any electrons & are already stable. They have no urge to destabilize themselves through gain or loss of electrons.
Greater the value of E.A., more electronegative or more oxidising is the element.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → E.A. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.A. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall E.A. DECREASES.
trend_down_a_group.note: Cl has higher E.A. than F (exception) because F has very small size with high electron-electron repulsion.

section_I_electronegativity.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Electronegativity (E.N.)
section_I_electronegativity.definition: The tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons to itself when combined in a compound.
bond_type_based_on_EN: IONIC BOND forms between combining atoms if atoms differ widely in electronegativity.
COVALENT BOND forms between combining atoms if atoms have nearly similar electronegativities to attract the bond forming electron pair.
factors_affecting_EN: Reasons affecting electronegativity are the same and in the same order as electron affinity.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → E.N. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.N. INCREASES
key_facts: Elements with high electronegativity are usually NON-METALLIC. (Non-metals are electronegative; metals are electropositive.)
Fluorine is the MOST electronegative element in the periodic table; Caesium is the LEAST.
In period 3, chlorine is the most electronegative element.
Noble gases have complete octet & hence do not attract electrons to themselves.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → E.N. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.N. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall E.N. DECREASES.

section_J_metallic_non_metallic_characte.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Metallic & Non-metallic Character

definitions.definition: In terms of electron LOSING property - an atom is a METAL if it loses one or more electrons when supplied with energy. M → M+ + e-
In terms of electron GAINING property - an atom is a NON-METAL if it gains one or more electrons when supplied with energy. N + e- → N-

key_facts: Metallic atoms (left side of periodic table) have LARGE atomic radii & LOW I.P., tend to LOSE electrons.
Non-metallic atoms (right side of periodic table) have SMALL atomic radii & HIGH I.P., tend to GAIN electrons.
Metals are good REDUCING agents; non-metals are good OXIDISING agents.
REACTIVITY of metals: greater the tendency to lose electrons, greater the reactivity.
REACTIVITY of non-metals: greater the tendency to gain electrons, greater the reactivity.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → metallic character DECREASES; non-metallic character INCREASES
I.P. INCREASES → metallic character DECREASES; non-metallic character INCREASES
Atomic radii INCREASE → metallic character INCREASES; non-metallic character DECREASES
I.P. DECREASES → metallic character INCREASES; non-metallic character DECREASES
trend_down_a_group.key_note: Elements at the BOTTOM of a group are MOST metallic - have large atomic size, lowest I.P., electrons are loosely held & will form ions from metals most readily & thus are more reactive.

physical_properties.across_a_period: Density & m.p./b.p. of elements INCREASE gradually (slight decrease thereafter).
physical_properties.down_a_group: Density INCREASES gradually; m.p. & b.p. DECREASE gradually.

table.across_a_period: Varies from Strongly basic to Strongly acidic
table.down_a_group: Strongly basic to Basic (less basic to strongly basic)

table.across_a_period: Strongly basic to Amphoteric to Strongly acidic

stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.definition: n/p (neutron/proton) ratio determines stability of elements.
stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.stable: Light metals - elements with n/p ratio around 1 are stable. e.g. Na and K.
stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.unstable_radioactive: Heavy metals - elements with n/p ratio above 1.5 are considered radioactive unstable elements. e.g. uranium.

key_terms_glossary.definition: Tabular arrangement of elements in increasing order of their atomic numbers, showing periodic variation in properties.
Properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Seven horizontal rows of the periodic table. Period number = number of electron shells in element.
Eighteen vertical columns of the periodic table. Group number (for main group) = number of valence electrons.
Groups 1, 2 & 13-17 (IA-VIIA). Also called representative or main group elements.
Groups 3-12 (IB-VIIB & VIII). Heavy metals with variable valency.
Lanthanides (period 6) and actinides (period 7) - 14 elements each, placed separately at bottom of periodic table.
Group 18 (0) elements with completely filled outer shell; unreactive; E.A. = 0.
Group 1 (IA) - highly reactive, soft, light metals; strong reducing agents; valency 1.
Group 2 (IIA) - reactive metals, harder than alkali metals; valency 2.
Group 17 (VIIA) - highly reactive non-metals; strong oxidising agents; valency 1.
Period 2 elements that show diagonal similarity with period 3 elements of the next group.
Period 3 elements that match the typical properties of their respective groups.
Recurrence of characteristic properties of elements at definite intervals (2, 8, 18, 32) in atomic number.
Distance between centre of nucleus and outermost shell of an atom. Unit = Å.
Positive charge on the nucleus of an atom; equivalent to atomic number.
Energy required to remove a loosely bound electron from outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
Energy released when an atom in gaseous state accepts an electron to form an anion.
Tendency of an atom to attract shared pair of electrons to itself when combined in a compound.
Tendency of an atom to lose electrons; high for metals.
Tendency of an atom to gain electrons; high for non-metals.
Substance that loses electrons (gets oxidised) and reduces another substance. Metals are good reducing agents.
Substance that gains electrons (gets reduced) and oxidises another substance. Non-metals (especially halogens) are good oxidising agents.
Property of an element to form chains by bonding with itself; notable in carbon (group 14).
Groups of three elements where atomic weight of middle is average of other two.
Every eighth element repeats properties of the first when arranged by atomic weight.
Atoms of same element with same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Neutron-to-proton ratio; stable elements ≈ 1; radioactive elements > 1.5.
Oxide that shows both acidic and basic properties (e.g. Al2O3).

mcqs.question: The energy required to remove an electron from a neutral isolated gaseous atom & convert it into a positively charged gaseous ion is called ___
mcqs.answer: Ionisation potential

mcqs.question: The most electronegative element from the following: A. Magnesium  B. Chlorine  C. Aluminium  D. Sulphur
mcqs.answer: B. Chlorine

mcqs.question: The element with highest ionization potential is: A. Hydrogen  B. Caesium  C. Radon  D. Helium
mcqs.answer: D. Helium

mcqs.question: In the Periodic Table, elements of Period 3 are arranged in increasing order of ionization potential as:
mcqs.answer: b. Mg, Si, S, Ar

mcqs.question: The tendency of an atom to attract shared pair of electrons to itself when forming a chemical bond is known as:
mcqs.answer: b. Electronegativity

mcqs.answer: d. B2A3 (A=Oxygen with valency 2; B=Aluminium with valency 3 → Al2O3)

give_reasons.question: Inert gases do not form ions.
give_reasons.answer: Inert gases have stable electronic configuration with completely filled outer shell (duplet or octet). They have no urge to destabilize themselves through gain or loss of electrons. They have zero electron affinity and very high ionisation potential, so they do not form ions.

give_reasons.question: Ionisation potential increases across a period from left to right.
give_reasons.answer: Across a period, atomic radii decreases (number of shells remains same, nuclear charge increases). Smaller atomic size means stronger nuclear attraction on outer electrons, making them harder to remove. Hence I.P. increases.

give_reasons.question: Ionisation potential decreases down a group.
give_reasons.answer: Down a group, atomic radii increases (more shells added). Larger atomic size means weaker nuclear attraction on outer electrons, making them easier to remove. Although nuclear charge increases, the increase in atomic size dominates. Hence I.P. decreases.

give_reasons.question: Noble gases are considered unreactive elements.
give_reasons.answer: Noble gases have completely filled outer shells (duplet for He, octet for others). They have zero electron affinity, very high ionisation potential, and no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons. Hence they are unreactive.

give_reasons.question: In a sub-group, the chemical properties of elements remain similar.
give_reasons.answer: Elements in the same sub-group have the same number of valence electrons (same outer electronic configuration). Since chemical properties depend on outer electronic configuration, elements in a sub-group have similar chemical properties.

give_reasons.question: Halogens in group 17 are strong oxidising agents.
give_reasons.answer: Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) have 7 valence electrons and need only 1 more electron to complete their octet. They have high electron affinity and high electronegativity, so they readily accept electrons from other substances. Substances that gain electrons are oxidising agents, hence halogens are strong oxidising agents.

give_reasons.question: Atomic radii is considered a periodic property, exhibiting periodicity.
give_reasons.answer: Atomic size varies in a regular pattern across periods and down groups, repeating at definite intervals of atomic number (2, 8, 18, 32). When elements with similar valence shell electronic configuration recur, they show similar atomic size patterns. Hence atomic radii is a periodic property.

give_reasons.question: Atomic size of neon is more than the atomic size of fluorine.
give_reasons.answer: Neon has a completely filled outer shell (octet). This results in a force of repulsion between the electrons, increasing the atomic size. The effect of nuclear pull over valence shell electrons is not seen. Hence Ne has a larger atomic radius than F.

give_reasons.question: In period 3, the most metallic element is sodium (not magnesium or aluminium).
give_reasons.answer: Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right. Sodium (group 1) is leftmost in period 3, has the largest atomic size and lowest I.P., making it the most metallic element in period 3.

give_reasons.question: Fluorine is the most electronegative element of the periodic table.
give_reasons.answer: Fluorine has the smallest atomic size among halogens (group 17) and the highest nuclear charge per shell (effective). It needs only 1 electron to complete its octet. With small size + high nuclear attraction, F has the highest tendency to attract shared electrons - hence most electronegative.

give_reasons.question: Phosphorus, sulphur & chlorine are electronegative elements of the periodic table.
give_reasons.answer: These elements are in the right side of period 3 (groups 15, 16, 17). They have small atomic size and high nuclear charge, so they tend to gain electrons (electronegative character). Non-metals are electronegative.

give_reasons.question: Chlorine is more metallic in nature than argon (placed at the extreme right of period 3).
give_reasons.answer: Metallic character decreases across a period. Argon (group 18) is rightmost in period 3 and is a noble gas with no metallic character. Chlorine (group 17) is to the left of argon, so it has slightly more metallic character than argon (though both are non-metals).

give_reasons.question: Sulphur is placed in group 16.
give_reasons.answer: Sulphur (16S) has electronic configuration 2,8,6 - it has 6 valence electrons. Group number (for main group elements) = number of valence electrons. Hence sulphur is placed in group 16.

give_reasons.question: Occurrence of characteristic properties of elements takes place at definite intervals in the modern periodic table.
give_reasons.answer: After definite intervals of atomic number (2, 8, 18, 32), elements with similar valence shell electronic configuration recur. Since properties depend on valence shell configuration, characteristic properties reappear at these intervals.

give_reasons.question: Properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers and not atomic weights.
give_reasons.answer: Physical and chemical properties of elements depend on the number of electrons and their arrangement (electronic configuration), which is determined by atomic number. Atomic weight does not correlate directly with electronic configuration. Hence properties are periodic functions of atomic numbers.

give_reasons.question: Atomic size of an element depends on the nuclear charge of that element.
give_reasons.answer: Nuclear charge (= atomic number) determines the force of attraction on electrons. Higher nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, decreasing atomic size. Lower nuclear charge means weaker pull, increasing atomic size. Hence atomic size depends on nuclear charge.

give_reasons.question: Down a group electronegativity should increase with increase in nuclear charge but it is seen that electronegativity decreases.
give_reasons.answer: Down a group, although nuclear charge increases, the number of electron shells also increases, making atomic size larger. The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and the nuclear pull is reduced. The increase in atomic size dominates over the increase in nuclear charge, hence electronegativity decreases.

give_reasons.question: If combining atoms have nearly similar electronegativities, the bond between them is covalent.
give_reasons.answer: When combining atoms have similar electronegativities, neither atom can completely pull the bonding electrons away from the other. So they share electrons (rather than transferring), forming a covalent bond. Large differences in electronegativity lead to ionic bonds.

give_reasons.question: Atomic size of group 18 (0 group) elements is more than that of group 17 elements.
give_reasons.answer: Group 18 elements (noble gases) have completely filled outer shells. This causes a force of repulsion between the electrons, expanding the atomic size. The nuclear pull on valence electrons is not as effective as in group 17 elements. Hence noble gases have larger atomic size than halogens of the same period.

quick_revision_summary.one_line_summary: Periodic table arranges elements by atomic number; across a period (L→R): size↓, I.P.↑, E.A.↑, E.N.↑, metallic character↓, non-metallic character↑. Down a group: size↑, I.P.↓, E.A.↓, E.N.↓, metallic character↑, non-metallic character↓.
quick_revision_summary.mnemonic_across_period: Across a period - 'MAGIC MEN' → Metallic character Decreases, Atomic size Decreases, I.P. Increases, Character (non-metallic) Increases. Then 'E3' → E.A., E.N., Electropositive (decreases) — All follow the trend: Across period: small atoms → strong pull → high I.P./E.A./E.N.
quick_revision_summary.mnemonic_down_group: Down a group - 'BIG MAC' → Big size, Increases metallic character. The rest (I.P., E.A., E.N., non-metallic character) all Decrease.
quick_revision_summary.trends_grid_compact:
Property           | Across Period (→) | Down Group (↓)
-------------------|-------------------|----------------
Atomic size        | Decreases          | Increases
I.P.               | Increases          | Decreases
E.A.               | Increases          | Decreases
E.N.               | Increases          | Decreases
Metallic char.     | Decreases          | Increases
Non-metallic char. | Increases          | Decreases
key_extremes: Highest I.P. = Helium (He); Lowest I.P. = Caesium (Cs)
Most electronegative = Fluorine (F, EN=4.0); Least electronegative = Caesium (Cs)
Highest E.A. = Chlorine (Cl, −3.80 eV); E.A. = 0 for noble gases
Largest atom (among main group) = Caesium (Cs); Smallest atom = Helium (He)
Most reactive metal = Cs (or Fr if radioactive); Most reactive non-metal = F
Best reducing agent (among alkali metals) = Li (due to high hydration energy) — per textbook note: Li is best reducing agent due to small size + high E.N. + high I.P.
exam_tips: Memorize the trends grid - this is the single most important table for the exam.
For 'give reasons' questions: state the cause (atomic size / nuclear charge / shells) → mechanism → result.
Noble gases are SPECIAL - they have: zero E.A., highest I.P. in period, larger atomic size than halogens.
Period number = number of shells. Group number (for main group) = number of valence electrons.
Across period: shells SAME, valence electrons INCREASE by 1.
Down group: shells INCREASE by 1, valence electrons SAME.
When asked to 'arrange in order': check if it's PERIOD elements (use across-period trend) or GROUP elements (use down-group trend).
Bridge elements = period 2 elements showing diagonal similarity with period 3 elements of NEXT group (e.g. Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si).
Hydrogen is unique - can be placed in group 1 (loses 1 e-) or group 17 (gains 1 e-).
Remember: small atom → strong nuclear pull → high I.P., high E.A., high E.N. (for non-metals).
Metals: large size, low I.P., lose electrons, reducing agents, basic oxides.
Non-metals: small size, high I.P., gain electrons, oxidising agents, acidic oxides.
For atomic size comparison: cation < parent atom < anion (e.g. Na+ < Na < Cl- in size).
Don't forget: Cl has HIGHER E.A. than F (exception due to small size of F causing electron-electron repulsion).

sections.title: Introduction & History of Classification
need_for_classification: Need arose to group elements into families whose elements showed maximum resemblance.
On such an arrangement in the form of a table, properties of elements were seen to reappear at regular intervals.

history_of_classification.outcome: Method discarded as elements showed variable valency and dual character.
Elements arranged in groups of three called TRIADS. Atomic weight of the middle element was generally the average of the other two. Discarded as it did not hold true for all elements.
Elements arranged in a series of eight. Properties of every eighth element were a repetition of the first (Law of Octaves). Discarded as it failed to leave spaces for undiscovered elements.

Elements arranged in the form of a table called Mendeleeff's Periodic Table. Stated that properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic weights. Could not justify position of certain elements, rare earths and isotopes.

Elements arranged in a modified table called Modern Periodic Table. Stated that properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Removes most defects of Mendeleeff's Periodic Table.

sections.title: Modern Periodic Table - Long form of the Periodic Table
introduction: Mendeleeff had arranged elements in the periodic table on basis of increasing atomic weights.

Moseley modified Mendeleeff's periodic table & stated that the basis of classification of elements should be increasing atomic numbers (not atomic weights) since physical and chemical properties of elements depend on the number of electrons and their arrangement.
Atomic number is equal to the number of electrons in the energy shells of an atom - hence atomic number is the fundamental property of an element.
sections.modern_periodic_law: Physical & chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

salient_features.description: Periodic table based on basic fundamental property - atomic number.
Correlates position of an element with its electronic configuration.
Arranges elements in increasing order of atomic numbers in SEVEN horizontal rows called PERIODS & EIGHTEEN vertical columns called GROUPS.

Completion of each period is logical - each period begins with an element having one electron in outermost shell & ends with zero group element having completely filled outer shell. A transition from metallic to non-metallic character is seen across a period.

Each vertical column accommodates elements with the same outer electronic configuration, hence having similar properties. 18 vertical columns consist of groups 1 to 17 & 18 [zero group]. Groups 1, 2 & 13 to 17 [IA to VIIA] are called NORMAL ELEMENTS. Groups 3 to 12 [IB to VIIB & VIII] are called TRANSITION ELEMENTS. Group 18 [zero] at extreme right contains NOBLE or INERT GASES.
Reactive metals placed in group 1 [IA] and 2 [IIA]. Transition elements [metals] placed in the middle. Non-metals placed in the upper right corner of the periodic table.

Gradual change in properties is seen with increase in atomic number. Periodicity in properties (recurrence of properties) is seen with elements of the same subgroup after a difference of 2, 8, 18 or 32 in atomic numbers - due to recurrence of similar valence shell electronic configuration.

sections.title: Periods in the Modern Periodic Table
key_concepts: Periods = Seven horizontal rows of elements arranged in increasing order of atomic numbers.
Period numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) signify the NUMBER OF ELECTRON SHELLS of an element.
Period 1 elements (e.g. 1H) have 1 shell; Period 2 elements (e.g. 3Li) have 2 shells; Period 3 elements (e.g. 11Na) have 3 shells, and so on.
sections.dual_position_of_hydrogen: Hydrogen has the simplest electronic configuration of one. It can hence lose 1 electron, behaving like alkali metals (group 1) OR gain 1 electron, behaving like halogens (group 17). It is hence placed above Li in group 1 OR above F in group 17.
sections.isotopes_of_hydrogen: Atoms of the same element, having same atomic number but different atomic mass numbers. Hydrogen exists in 3 isotopic forms: 1H, 2H, 3H. Since they have the same electronic configuration, they occupy the same position in the periodic table.

bridge_elements.definition: Period 2 elements are called 'bridge elements' - they show similarities in properties diagonally with the period 3 element of the next group.

Period 2:  Li  Be  B  C   (bridge elements)

Period 3:  Na  Mg  Al  Si  (typical elements)
bridge_elements.example: Li (period 2, group 1) shows diagonal similarity with Mg (period 3, group 2).

property_trends_across_a_period.trend: REMAINS SAME (electrons enter same shell - K, L, M)
INCREASES BY ONE (from left to right)
INCREASES (transition from metallic to non-metallic character)

sections.title: Groups in the Modern Periodic Table
key_concepts: Groups = Eighteen vertical columns (with eight main groups) in the periodic table.
Group numbers signify the NUMBER OF VALENCE ELECTRONS of an element (valence electrons = electrons in outermost shell).
Group 1 (IA) elements e.g. 11Na [2,8,1] have 1 valence electron.
Group 2 (IIA) elements e.g. 12Mg [2,8,2] have 2 valence electrons, and so on.
Transition elements also have 2 valence electrons - e.g. 26Fe [2,8,14,2], 30Zn [2,8,18,2].

groups_summary_table.elements: Heavy metals from 21Sc to 30Zn; 39Y to 48Cd; 72Hf to 80Hg

sections.inner_transition_elements_note: INNER TRANSITION ELEMENTS (e.g. 58Ce, 90Th) - Metals. Lanthanides (rare earths) & Actinides (radioactive) - two series of 14 elements each. Form two horizontal rows at the bottom of the periodic table. They lie between strongly electropositive metals on the left & least electropositive elements on the right. All have 3 valence electrons (e.g. 21Sc [2,8,8,3]).

property_trends_down_a_subgroup.trend: REMAIN SIMILAR (or vary gradually) - because chemical properties depend on outer electronic configuration

group_1_alkali_metals.elements: Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), Rubidium (Rb), Caesium (Cs), Francium (Fr)
group_1_alkali_metals.nature: Highly reactive, highly electropositive, light, soft metals. Metallic in nature. Soft - can be cut with a knife.
group_1_alkali_metals.redox_nature: Strong reducing agents (alkali metals are electron donors). Have one valence electron easily removed from outer shell. After loss, achieve stable configuration of noble gases.
group_1_alkali_metals.electronegativity: Low electronegativity (electropositive character increases from Li to Cs)

group_17_halogen.nature: Highly reactive, highly electronegative, non-metals. Non-metallic in nature. Gaseous: F & Cl; Liquid: Br; Solid at room temp: I
group_17_halogen.conductivity: Bad or non-conductors of heat & electricity
group_17_halogen.redox_nature: Strong oxidising agents (halogens are electron acceptors). Electronegative character decreases from F to I.
group_17_halogen.reaction_with_non_metals: Covalent compounds formed (e.g. HCl, PCl3, SCl4)
group_17_halogen.reaction_with_hydrogen: Covalent hydrides formed (e.g. HF, HCl, HBr, HI)

sections.title: Periodic Properties - Variation in Periods & Groups

periodicity_in_properties.definition: Occurrence of characteristic properties of elements at definite intervals in the modern periodic table when elements are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers. (Definite intervals = difference of 2, 8, 18 or 32 in atomic numbers.)
periodicity_in_properties.modern_periodic_law: Properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

reasons_for_periodicity: After definite intervals of atomic number, similar valence shell electronic configuration occurs.
Properties of elements depend on the number & arrangement of electrons in various shells including valence shell.
In the same period or subgroup, increase or decrease in a particular property is due to gradual change in electronic configuration in the arranged elements.

definitions_table.definition: It is the distance between the centre of the nucleus and the outermost shell of the atom.
It is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
It is the amount of energy released when an atom in the gaseous state accepts an electron to form an anion.
definitions_table.equation: X + e- → X- + energy liberated  [Energy released = E.A.]

definitions_table.definition: It is the tendency of an atom to attract electrons to itself when combined in a compound.
definitions_table.note: Small difference in E.N. between combining atoms → covalent bond. Large difference → ionic bond.

definitions_table.definition: In terms of electron loss or gain: an element is a Non-metal if it gains one or more electrons; a Metal if it loses one or more electrons.

sections.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Atomic Size
sections.definition: The distance between the centre of the nucleus of an atom and its outermost shell. (Atomic radius determines bond length.) Unit = Angstrom (Å).

factors_affecting_atomic_size.effect: Increases → Atomic size INCREASES. Reason: distance of outermost shell from nucleus increases.
Increases → Atomic size DECREASES. Reason: electrons in outermost shell are attracted with increasing force. (Nuclear charge = positive charge on nucleus = atomic number of element.)

reasons: Number of shells REMAINS SAME → atomic size unaffected
Nuclear charge INCREASES → atomic size DECREASES

example_period_2.note: Larger than F since outer shell completely filled → force of repulsion; nuclear pull not seen

key_facts: In period 2, Li has the LARGEST atomic radius & F has the SMALLEST.
Neon has a larger atomic radius since in inert gases the outer shell is completely filled, resulting in a force of repulsion. The effect of nuclear pull over valence shell electrons is not seen.
A cation (e.g. Na → Na+ + e-) is SMALLER than the parent neutral atom since the remaining electrons are strongly attracted by the nucleus.

reasons: Number of shells INCREASES → atomic size INCREASES (new shells added with increasing atomic number; nuclear distance from valence electrons increases).
Nuclear charge should increase → atomic size should decrease. BUT
Increase in number of shells DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall atomic radius INCREASES.
trend_down_a_group.important_note: From Li, Na & K - Li has the smallest atomic radius & therefore has higher E.N. & I.P. compared to Na & K. Hence Li has a greater tendency to lose electrons, making it the BEST reducing agent.

sections.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Ionisation Potential (I.P.)
sections.definition: The amount of energy required to remove a loosely bound electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
first_and_second_IP: Energy required to remove 1st electron = FIRST I.P. (M → M+ + e-)  [first I.P. is less]
Energy required to remove 2nd electron = SECOND I.P. (M+ → M2+ + e-)  [second I.P. is more]

factors_affecting_IP.effect: Increases → I.P. DECREASES. Reason: nuclear attraction on outer electrons decreases; outer electrons loosely held.
Increases → I.P. INCREASES. Reason: nuclear attraction on outer electrons increases; outer electrons firmly held.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → I.P. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → I.P. INCREASES
key_facts: Helium (He) has the HIGHEST ionisation potential; Caesium (Cs) has the LOWEST (Francium is radioactive).
Neon in period 2 also has maximum I.P. since its outer shell is completely filled.
Metals lose electrons & generally have LOW ionisation potential compared to non-metals.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → I.P. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → I.P. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall I.P. DECREASES.

sections.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Electron Affinity (E.A.)
sections.definition: The amount of energy released when an atom in the gaseous state accepts an electron to form an anion.
equations: X + e- → X- + energy liberated  [1st electron affinity]
Cl + e- → Cl-  [−3.80 eV, represented with −ve sign]

factors_affecting_EA.effect: Increases → E.A. DECREASES. Reason: A small atom takes up electrons more readily than a large atom since nucleus has greater attraction on the electrons.
Increases → E.A. INCREASES. Reason: increases the tendency of the atom to accept electrons.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → E.A. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.A. INCREASES
key_facts: Electron affinity is HIGHEST for halogens (group 17) & LEAST for alkali metals (group 1).
Neon (Ne) has electron affinity ZERO since inert gases with stable electronic configuration find it difficult to accept electrons.

INERT GASES DO NOT FORM IONS - their outermost shell is completely filled. They need not accept or donate any electrons & are already stable. They have no urge to destabilize themselves through gain or loss of electrons.
Greater the value of E.A., more electronegative or more oxidising is the element.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → E.A. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.A. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall E.A. DECREASES.
trend_down_a_group.note: Cl has higher E.A. than F (exception) because F has very small size with high electron-electron repulsion.

sections.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Electronegativity (E.N.)
sections.definition: The tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons to itself when combined in a compound.
bond_type_based_on_EN: IONIC BOND forms between combining atoms if atoms differ widely in electronegativity.
COVALENT BOND forms between combining atoms if atoms have nearly similar electronegativities to attract the bond forming electron pair.
factors_affecting_EN: Reasons affecting electronegativity are the same and in the same order as electron affinity.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → E.N. INCREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.N. INCREASES
key_facts: Elements with high electronegativity are usually NON-METALLIC. (Non-metals are electronegative; metals are electropositive.)
Fluorine is the MOST electronegative element in the periodic table; Caesium is the LEAST.
In period 3, chlorine is the most electronegative element.
Noble gases have complete octet & hence do not attract electrons to themselves.

reasons: Atomic radii INCREASE (no. of shells increases) → E.N. DECREASES
Nuclear charge INCREASES → E.N. should increase. BUT
Increase in atomic radii DOMINATES over increase in nuclear charge. Overall E.N. DECREASES.

sections.title: Periodic Trends in Properties - Metallic & Non-metallic Character

definitions.definition: In terms of electron LOSING property - an atom is a METAL if it loses one or more electrons when supplied with energy. M → M+ + e-
In terms of electron GAINING property - an atom is a NON-METAL if it gains one or more electrons when supplied with energy. N + e- → N-

key_facts: Metallic atoms (left side of periodic table) have LARGE atomic radii & LOW I.P., tend to LOSE electrons.
Non-metallic atoms (right side of periodic table) have SMALL atomic radii & HIGH I.P., tend to GAIN electrons.
Metals are good REDUCING agents; non-metals are good OXIDISING agents.
REACTIVITY of metals: greater the tendency to lose electrons, greater the reactivity.
REACTIVITY of non-metals: greater the tendency to gain electrons, greater the reactivity.

reasons: Atomic radii DECREASE → metallic character DECREASES; non-metallic character INCREASES
I.P. INCREASES → metallic character DECREASES; non-metallic character INCREASES
Atomic radii INCREASE → metallic character INCREASES; non-metallic character DECREASES
I.P. DECREASES → metallic character INCREASES; non-metallic character DECREASES
trend_down_a_group.key_note: Elements at the BOTTOM of a group are MOST metallic - have large atomic size, lowest I.P., electrons are loosely held & will form ions from metals most readily & thus are more reactive.

physical_properties.across_a_period: Density & m.p./b.p. of elements INCREASE gradually (slight decrease thereafter).
physical_properties.down_a_group: Density INCREASES gradually; m.p. & b.p. DECREASE gradually.

table.across_a_period: Varies from Strongly basic to Strongly acidic
table.down_a_group: Strongly basic to Basic (less basic to strongly basic)

stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.definition: n/p (neutron/proton) ratio determines stability of elements.
stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.stable: Light metals - elements with n/p ratio around 1 are stable. e.g. Na and K.
stable_vs_unstable_elements_reference.unstable_radioactive: Heavy metals - elements with n/p ratio above 1.5 are considered radioactive unstable elements. e.g. uranium.
